why: How the latency gate decides whether this build is slower than the last release. It holds the tolerance and the protocol, and — since document_version 2 — no measurements at all: nothing is recorded at release time, because the thing this build is compared against is the previous release's CODE, which the repository already has.
tolerance_why: 8% is the room a regression has to clear to be called one. On the paired protocol below it is about four times the noise: both sides are measured on one machine, back to back, so what is left is within-process spread — 0.7% in Python, 1.7% in Ruby, 3.3% in TypeScript — and the median over several rounds is tighter than that. The same 8% under the stored baseline this replaces was about a third of the noise, which is why it failed unchanged code.
protocol: paired, same machine, interleaved and counterbalanced: tools/latency_pair.py checks the previous release out into a worktree, measures it and this checkout alternately for several rounds, and writes both medians to a record the gate reads. Every property of the machine is common to both sides and cancels.
protocol_why: Because the machine is not a constant, and a stored number assumes it is. Thirty-six processes across six GitHub ubuntu-latest runners per port, on IDENTICAL code, spread 67% in Ruby (6.53 ms on an Intel Xeon 6973P-C against 10.63 ms on an EPYC 7763), 26% in Python and 21% in TypeScript. One probe run drew five CPU models from that single runner label — EPYC 7763, EPYC 9V74, Xeon Platinum 8370C, Xeon Platinum 8573C, Xeon 6973P-C — and two runners of the SAME model still differed by 26%. A stored baseline therefore decided releases by which machine the job landed on: it red-lit main on unchanged code at +8.33%, having already refused RubyGems 0.2.3 while PyPI and npm took the same commit. Two cheaper repairs were measured first and rejected: a full warmup pass (kept, because it fixes a real TypeScript-only distortion, but it only touches the within-runner term) and dividing by a machine-speed calibrator (helped Ruby, hurt TypeScript, left 18-25% residual spread).
rounds_why: Rounds per side, bought where they are needed rather than spread evenly. Five already puts Python and Ruby inside ±1%; TypeScript's per-process noise is 3.3% because its absolute figure is 2 ms and its JIT does not settle identically twice, and a measurement there costs about a third of a second, so it takes three times as many. A port measured to three times the noise of another is not held to the same gate.
estimator: median of every essay x every repeat, pooled — 20 essays x 5 repeats = 100 samples — after an untimed warmup pass over the whole corpus. NOT a percentile: at n=20 essays a p95 is the maximum, and a maximum moves on scheduling noise rather than on code.
estimator_why: The warmup is a full corpus pass rather than the single 200-char call it started as, because a runner measurement showed TypeScript's first four essays running at about TWICE their steady-state cost while V8 tiers the redaction path up. That put a quarter of the pooled samples above steady state and made the estimator's value depend on when the JIT happened to finish: 3.3% between processes on one machine, against 0.7% in Python. Python and Ruby barely move under it and do it anyway — three ports that estimate differently are three different gates.
corpus_why: Latency scales with essay length, so a measurement belongs to the corpus it was taken on. The pair harness holds conformance/ and asset/ fixed across both sides for the same reason, and each side prints a digest of the essay text it timed; the harness refuses to write a record when the two disagree.
